summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee; Anabel Eckerling; Boaz Israeli; Gali Yanovich; Ella Rosenne; Suzana Fichman-Horn; Ido Ben Zvi; Liat Sorski; Ronit Satchi-Fainaro; Tamar Geiger; Erica K Sloan; Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanism behind the rare clinical phenomenon of spontaneous metastatic regression following primary tumor (PT) excision. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-based xenograft model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor induces marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, but not larger established metastases. The study hypothesizes that the primary tumor secretes factors that support distant metastatic growth. By supplementing the tumor secretome in vivo after excision, the authors successfully reversed this regression, confirming the role of secreted factors. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key mediators: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested metastatic progression even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, high levels of these four proteins were correlated with poor survival in a cohort of lung adenocarcinoma patients from the TCGA dataset. The findings suggest that the perioperative period represents a critical window to control minimal residual disease by blocking primary tumor-derived pro-metastatic support.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanism behind the rare clinical phenomenon of spontaneous metastatic regression following primary tumor (PT) excision. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-based xenograft model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor induces marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, but not larger established metastases. The study hypothesizes that the primary tumor secretes factors that support distant metastatic growth. By supplementing the tumor secretome in vivo after excision, the authors successfully reversed this regression, confirming the role of secreted factors. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key mediators: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested metastatic progression even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, high levels of these four proteins were correlated with poor survival in a cohort of lung adenocarcinoma patients from the TCGA dataset. The findings suggest that the perioperative period represents a critical window to control minimal residual disease by blocking primary tumor-derived pro-metastatic support.

Research Context
Surgical removal is a cornerstone of cancer treatment. However, case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression. This phenomenon is most commonly reported for lung metastases. Proposed mechanisms include elimination of stimulating factors. However, no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Does primary tumor excision cause spontaneous regression of micro-metastases? Is this regression due to surgical trauma or removal of secreted factors? Does primary tumor secretome support distant metastatic growth? Can specific secreted factors be identified to mediate this effect? Does blocking these factors arrest metastasis in the presence of the PT?

Methodological Details
The study used MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells. Cells expressed highly sensitive luciferase for monitoring. Eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were used. Cells were injected into the fourth mammary fat pad. Primary tumors were measured by caliper. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging. Excision occurred when flux reached 10^6 photons/s. Tumor cell-conditioned medium (CM) was prepared in vitro. Alzet osmotic minipumps were used for in vivo supplementation. Human Cytokine Array (ARY022) analyzed 102 soluble proteins. Mass spectrometry identified 2,600 proteins in CM. Neutralizing antibodies targeted IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF. Patient data was drawn from the public TCGA provisional dataset.

Procedures And Architectures
Cells were cultured in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum. Mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12 h dark/light cycle. Primary tumors were excised under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Sham surgery involved an identical incision without tumor removal. CM was concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to 100 μl/mouse. Minipumps were implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. Adhesion studies used the IncuCyte system over 8 hours. Apoptosis was determined by AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD staining. Tube formation used human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC). Proteomics used MaxQuant with a false discovery rate of 0.01. Antibodies were injected once a day for two days. Survival analysis used Kaplan Meier Analysis and hazard ratios.

Key Results
Excision caused a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal. The decrease in signal was up to 100-fold. Regression was significant with p<0.0001. Metastases regressed into latent foci with no signal increase. Regression was specific to early stages, not larger metastases. Sham surgery showed continued increase in metastases. CM supplementation reduced regression by 10-fold. CM treatment showed p<0.005 compared to serum-free medium. Neutralization of four factors completely blocked progression. Antibody neutralization showed p<0.0001 significance. High protein levels correlated with poor survival in patients. The hazard ratio for poor survival was 2.05. The p-value for the survival correlation was <0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Primary tumor secretome supports survival of distant micro-metastases. Removal of the PT and its secreted factors induces regression. Larger micrometastases may be self-sufficient. Surgical trauma alone does not elicit regression of metastases. These factors act through multiple mechanisms to affect cells. The perioperative period could be exploited to control disease. Blocking factors may counteract metastasis-promoting effects of surgery. Findings explain the rare clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study used a xenograft model, not syngeneic lines. Only four key factors were tested for blockade. Other secreted factors are likely also involved. Generalizability to different tumors needs further testing. The prevalence of post-operative regression is currently unknown. Technical limitations hinder detection of this process in patients. The amount of secretome from pumps was estimated at ~1/8 in vivo.

Claims
Primary tumor secretome promotes early metastatic growth and its removal causes regression. Excision caused regression of micro-metastases. CM supplementation diminished this regression. CM reduced regression by 10-fold. Regression was not seen in larger metastases. Sham surgery did not cause regression. Novel approaches to control minimal residual disease. Perioperative blocking of secreted factors.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are key mediators of metastatic progression. Neutralization of these factors arrested progression. High levels correlated with poor survival. Hazard ratio was 2.05 for high levels. Other factors are likely involved. Targeting these factors may prevent metastasis. Individualized antibody combinations may be effective.

Data And Code Availability
Patient data was from the public TCGA provisional dataset. Proteomics data analysis used Perseus software.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation of four factors blocked progression in the presence of PT. Sensitivity analysis showed regression specific to early stages.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by ethics committees.

Three Takeaways
Primary tumor secretome drives early metastatic growth. Neutralizing four factors arrests metastasis in vivo. Perioperative blockade offers a therapeutic window.
